items.passage: A drawer of lead type slid open with a groan when Hamza needed the letter that, in our shared wall's language of knocks, meant come over. I had lived beside his printing press in Beirut for six years and knew its moods: the thump of the platen, the hiss of the ink roller, the mutter of a man who disliked every street map he had ever printed. That evening he spread a new one across his table and jabbed at the errors, a missing alley here, a renamed square there, until I, Mehreen, began to defend the city's mapmakers out of pure stubbornness. Then he traced a faint pencil line I had not noticed. It ran from my door to his, through the plaster. "This," he said, "they always leave out." I stopped arguing.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the passage?
options: It shifts from bitter resentment to forgiveness as the narrator finally pardons Hamza's many insults.
It shifts from bickering humor to quiet tenderness when Hamza reveals the line between their homes.
It shifts from nostalgic longing to practical urgency as the neighbors correct the map's mistakes.
It shifts from fearful suspicion to trust when the narrator learns the purpose of the knocking.
items.explanation: 앞부분은 Hamza가 지도의 오류를 찌르고 화자가 고집으로 지도 제작자를 변호하는 티격태격하는 유머가 중심이다. 그러나 Hamza가 화자의 집에서 자기 집으로 이어지는 연필 선을 보여 주며 '그들은 늘 이걸 빼먹는다'고 말하자 화자는 말다툼을 멈춘다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A의 원한과 D의 의심은 지문에 없고, C는 결말의 정서를 잘못 짚었다.

items.passage: Three things were forbidden in the Gdansk library where my aunt Ksenia worked: food, whispering, and the name Dmitri. I was fifteen, cooking her dinners that winter, and I broke the first rule constantly, smuggling dumplings in my coat to eat between the stacks. Ksenia scolded me in her flat librarian's voice and confiscated them with the same efficiency she used for overdue books. I thought her made of index cards. One evening, shelving a returned atlas, I found a slip tucked inside: a borrower's card, decades old, signed Dmitri in a child's looping script. Beneath it, in Ksenia's neat hand, someone had renewed the loan every year. I carried it to her desk. She looked at it for a long time, and her voice, when it came, was barely a whisper.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the passage?
options: It shifts from fearful obedience to rebellious defiance as the narrator breaks the library rules.
It shifts from warm affection to cold suspicion when the narrator uncovers Ksenia's secret.
It shifts from wry amusement at Ksenia's strictness to solemn recognition of her hidden grief.
It shifts from somber mourning to lighthearted relief once the forgotten name is spoken aloud.
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 화자는 만두를 몰래 들여오고 고모를 '색인 카드로 만든 사람'이라 여기는 등 고모의 엄격함을 가볍게 비꼰다. 그러나 매년 대출이 연장된 Dmitri의 오래된 카드를 발견하고, 엄격하던 고모가 겨우 속삭이듯 말하는 장면에서 숨겨진 슬픔을 엄숙하게 깨닫는 어조로 바뀐다. 따라서 C가 정답이다. A는 반항, B는 의심으로 잘못 해석했고, D는 순서와 정서가 모두 반대다.

items.passage: Spools of thread rattled in Baoyu's tin as she climbed into the old projection booth above the shuttered cinema in Chengdu, where she had sewn costumes for twenty years. Hari, her only apprentice, was already there, pinning hems by the dusty window. The theater's owner had sold the building; one of them could follow him to his new shop across the river, and one could not. Baoyu had rehearsed the speech for days. Instead, she watched Hari work. He knotted thread the way she had taught him, then in a way she hadn't, a small twist that held better than hers. She remembered her own teacher, decades earlier, watching her the same way before stepping aside. When the owner climbed the stairs, Baoyu set the tin of spools in Hari's hands and turned to the projector.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?
options: It describes a conflict between two workers, then shows them agreeing to share a new shop.
It presents the long history of a cinema, then explains why its owner decided to sell the building.
It contrasts two sewing techniques, then argues that the older method is superior.
It introduces a difficult choice, then traces the observations that lead Baoyu to resolve it.
items.explanation: 지문은 둘 중 한 명만 주인을 따라갈 수 있다는 어려운 선택을 먼저 제시한다. 이어 Baoyu가 Hari의 바느질을 지켜보며 그의 실력을 확인하고, 자신의 스승이 물러나던 기억을 떠올린 뒤 실패 통을 Hari에게 건넨다. 따라서 선택과 그 해결로 이끄는 관찰을 따라간다는 D가 정답이다. A의 공유, B의 극장 역사, C의 기법 우열 주장은 지문 구조와 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: By noon the line at Matteo's noodle stall in Bologna stretched past the fountain, and every customer obeyed the sign nailed above the counter: one bowl per person, no exceptions. Caio, who had taught Matteo arithmetic forty years before, reached the front and asked for two. Matteo pointed at the sign without looking up. "Rules are rules, maestro." Caio nodded, paid for one, and stepped aside. He did not leave. Instead he stood by the fountain and gave his bowl, untouched, to a boy whose mother had been turned away for asking the same thing. Matteo watched the boy eat. Then he watched the next customer, a widow with two grandchildren, reach the counter. He reached up, pried the sign loose, and slid it under the cash drawer, where flour soon covered it.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?
options: It establishes a rigid rule, shows a quiet act that exposes its cost, and ends with the rule being abandoned.
It describes a busy market, then shifts to a lengthy debate between two former classmates about the fairness of the stall's prices.
It recounts a teacher's lesson from the past, then shows a student applying it decades later.
It introduces a popular stall, then explains the economic reasons for limiting customers' orders.
items.explanation: 지문은 '한 사람당 한 그릇'이라는 엄격한 규칙으로 시작한다. 이어 Caio가 자신의 그릇을 거절당한 소년에게 건네는 조용한 행동으로 규칙의 대가를 드러내고, 마지막에 Matteo가 간판을 떼어 내 규칙을 포기한다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B의 가격 논쟁, C의 과거 수업 회상, D의 경제적 이유 설명은 지문에 나오지 않는다.

items.passage: I watched Renata glue the broken bowl at the ceramics studio in Valparaiso the spring I turned sixteen, and I told her, with all the scorn I could gather, that a mended bowl was still a broken one. She had married my father that winter; the bowl had been my mother's, and I had dropped it, not quite by accident. Renata did not argue. She filled the cracks with a gold-tinted resin and set the bowl on the kiln shelf to cure. For weeks I ignored it. Then Ximena, the studio's owner, asked me to carry it to the display window. In the afternoon light the seams looked less like damage than like a map. I still believe some things cannot be repaired. I have also kept the bowl on my desk for nine years.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?
options: It describes how to repair pottery, then argues that carefully repaired objects are always more valuable than new ones.
It recounts the narrator's early scorn for a repair, then traces a gradual and incomplete change in her view.
It presents a conflict between Renata and Ximena, then shows the narrator taking Ximena's side.
It opens with the narrator's present-day life, then flashes back to the day her mother left.
items.explanation: 화자는 처음에 수선한 그릇도 여전히 깨진 그릇이라며 경멸한다. 이후 몇 주 동안 무시하다가 진열창의 빛 아래에서 이음새가 지도처럼 보이는 경험을 하고, 여전히 고칠 수 없는 것이 있다고 믿으면서도 그릇을 9년간 간직한다. 따라서 경멸에서 점진적이고 불완전한 변화로 이어진다는 B가 정답이다. A는 수선 방법과 가치 주장으로, C는 인물 간 갈등으로, D는 시간 순서를 잘못 파악했다.

items.passage: When the Surabaya market opened at dawn, Arisa unrolled her mother's batik across the stall table before the fruit sellers had even lifted their shutters. Her mother, too weak now to walk the aisles, still drew the patterns each night in wax by lamplight, and Arisa dyed and sold them. Customers stopped all morning. They traced the waxy borders with their fingertips, called the work extraordinary, and photographed it for their cousins abroad. __A tourist asked whether the artist would sign one, then left without buying anything.__ By noon Arisa had sold two small scarves, enough for rice and her mother's medicine but not for the new wax. On the walk home she rehearsed what she would say, something about the praise, and decided to tell her mother only that people had loved the colors.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces a customer whose later purchase allows Arisa to buy wax for her mother.
It suggests that Arisa's mother is becoming famous among visitors from other countries.
It reveals that Arisa quietly resents the tourists because they misunderstand her mother's patterns.
It sharpens the contrast between the admiration the batik receives and the little money it earns.
items.explanation: 밑줄 친 문장 앞에서 손님들은 작품을 '대단하다'고 칭찬하며 사진을 찍고, 밑줄 문장에서는 관광객이 서명까지 청하고도 아무것도 사지 않는다. 뒤이어 정오까지 작은 스카프 두 장만 팔려 밀랍 살 돈이 부족하다는 내용이 나온다. 따라서 이 문장은 칭찬과 적은 수입의 대비를 날카롭게 한다는 D가 정답이다. A는 그 관광객이 물건을 사지 않았으므로 틀렸고, B는 명성, C는 원망으로 과장했다.

items.passage: Lindiwe had always translated for her father at the beekeeper's yard in Addis Ababa, turning buyers' English into his Zulu and back again, smoothing his blunt prices into polite offers. He trusted her completely, and she liked being trusted. Then, in March, her teacher returned an essay about the hives with a single comment: You write as if you are apologizing for him. Lindiwe read it on the bus and again at the gate. __That afternoon, when a buyer called the honey too expensive, she repeated her father's answer word for word: "Then buy cheaper honey."__ Thandiwe, her younger sister, gasped. Her father looked at her as though seeing a stranger, then laughed, a sound she had not heard from him in the yard before. The buyer paid the full price.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows Lindiwe acting on her teacher's remark by translating her father's words without softening them.
It reveals that Lindiwe secretly disagrees with her father's high prices and wants the buyer to leave the yard.
It explains why the buyer later decides to purchase honey from a cheaper seller.
It establishes that Lindiwe has never before translated for her father in the yard.
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Lindiwe는 아버지의 투박한 가격 제시를 늘 부드럽게 다듬어 번역했고, 교사는 그녀가 아버지를 대신해 사과하는 것처럼 쓴다고 지적한다. 밑줄 친 문장에서 그녀는 처음으로 아버지의 말을 한 글자도 바꾸지 않고 전하며, 이는 아버지의 웃음과 구매자의 지불로 이어진다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B와 C는 결말과 맞지 않고, D는 그녀가 늘 통역해 왔다는 첫 문장과 모순된다.

items.passage: When I was twelve, Ephraim, my violin teacher, made me play scales among the cabbages in a community garden in Tromso, because, he said, plants did not flatter anyone. He was exacting to the point of cruelty: a slightly sour note meant starting the whole piece over. Somewhere in those years, he claimed, I had promised to play at the garden's midsummer supper. I did not remember any such promise, and I suspect he invented it. __Still, I practiced that summer as I never had before, with Yiannis, the gardener, nodding along between the rows.__ On the night of the supper, my bow trembled on the first note and steadied on the second. I have since forgotten nearly everything I played. I remember the cabbages, enormous and blue in the long evening light.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It reveals that the narrator finally remembers making the promise to Ephraim.
It shows the narrator committing to a promise she doubts she ever made, preparing for the performance.
It suggests that Yiannis, rather than Ephraim, is the narrator's true teacher.
It criticizes Ephraim's strict methods by showing that the narrator stubbornly refused to practice at all.
items.explanation: 밑줄 문장 앞에서 화자는 그런 약속을 기억하지 못하며 선생님이 지어냈다고 의심한다. 그런데도 밑줄 문장에서 그 어느 때보다 열심히 연습했다고 말하고, 이어 한여름 만찬에서의 연주 장면이 나온다. 따라서 의심스러운 약속을 지키기로 하고 연주를 준비하는 모습을 보여 준다는 B가 정답이다. A는 '여전히 기억하지 못한다'는 맥락과, D는 열심히 연습했다는 내용과 모순되며, C는 근거가 없다.

items.passage: "You're the ranger who closed the ridge trail," Koa said, still breathing hard at the cemetery gate where the search party had found him. Bokhee, who had spent four hours in Auckland's drizzle looking for him, did not answer at once. The narrator of this town's small dramas, I watched from the caretaker's shed. Koa had come to scatter his grandfather's ashes on the ridge, and he had missed the one clear evening of the month. He blamed the closure; he blamed the map; he blamed Bokhee most of all. She let him. She handed him a thermos, then, when he had finished, a folded paper: the reopening date, written in her own hand, and a note that she would walk him up herself. I have seen many people argue with grief. Few of them meet anyone so patient.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Bokhee?
options: Amused, because the narrator finds her refusal to defend herself somewhat foolish.
Critical, because the narrator believes she closed the trail without good reason.
Admiring, because the narrator values her patient kindness toward a grieving man.
Indifferent, because the narrator watches the encounter only from a distance.
items.explanation: 서술자는 Bokhee가 Koa의 비난을 묵묵히 받아 주고 보온병을 건넨 뒤 직접 산행을 함께하겠다는 메모를 주는 장면을 자세히 보여 준다. 그리고 슬픔과 다투는 사람은 많지만 '그토록 인내심 있는' 사람을 만나는 이는 드물다고 평가한다. 두 단서를 연결하면 그녀의 인내와 친절을 높이 사는 C가 정답이다. 서술자가 멀리서 지켜보긴 하지만 평가를 담고 있으므로 D는 틀렸고, A와 B는 근거가 없다.

items.passage: I married Kian in April, and by June I was living in his mother's rented farmhouse outside Lima, waiting with her for a letter from the consulate that would decide whether he could return from abroad. Valentina did not like me; she said so plainly on my second day. She corrected how I folded the sheets and how I salted the beans. Yet each morning she walked the long road to the post office before I woke, and each morning she came back and told me, without being asked, that there was nothing yet. Once I found her asleep at the kitchen table with my mended blouse in her lap. I folded it the way she preferred and said nothing. I am still not sure whether she likes me. I no longer think it is the most important question.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Valentina?
options: Resentful, because the narrator feels that Valentina's criticism has made her unwelcome.
Fearful, because the narrator worries that Valentina will turn Kian against her.
Dismissive, because the narrator considers Valentina's household rules trivial and outdated.
Appreciative, because the narrator recognizes care beneath Valentina's blunt manner.
items.explanation: 화자는 Valentina가 자신을 싫어한다고 말하고 빨래 개는 법과 간 맞추는 법을 지적한다고 전한다. 그러나 매일 아침 먼저 우체국에 다녀와 소식을 알려 주고, 화자의 블라우스를 수선하다 잠든 모습을 보며 무뚝뚝함 아래의 배려를 알아본다. 화자가 그녀가 선호하는 방식으로 옷을 개는 데서 존중도 드러나므로 D가 정답이다. A는 초반 인상만 본 오답이고, B와 C는 근거가 없다.

items.passage:
Jamal laid the gift beside Shigeru's tray
in the dining hall of the Delta camp:
a pocketknife, worn smooth, his grandfather's.

I was the one who carried words between them,
and I chose the wrong ones, I think.
Shigeru heard keep this to cut ties
and set the knife down as if it burned.

All week the cicadas argued in the oaks.
All week the two of them ate at separate tables.

On the last night I tried again, slower,
the way you open a jar that has stuck:
keep this, so you can whittle a way back.
Shigeru turned the knife in the lamplight
and smiled the way a door opens.
items.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward her role in the misunderstanding?
options: Regretful but determined to repair the error she believes she made.
Defensive, insisting that the misunderstanding was Jamal's fault alone.
Detached, describing the conflict as though she played no part in it.
Amused by the confusion and unconcerned about its effect on the two men.
items.explanation: 화자는 통역자로서 '잘못된 말을 고른 것 같다'고 인정하며 자신의 실수를 후회한다. 이후 일주일 동안 두 사람이 따로 앉는 것을 지켜본 뒤 마지막 밤에 더 천천히 다시 통역을 시도해 오해를 바로잡는다. 따라서 후회하면서도 실수를 고치려는 A가 정답이다. B는 화자가 스스로 책임을 인정한 점과, C와 D는 그녀가 적극적으로 다시 시도한 점과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: When the monastery guesthouse in Manchester began clearing out its rooms, I took a job helping Grant, who ran the secondhand shop that bought the contents. Most of it went quickly: iron bedframes, hymnals, a box of mismatched spoons. The last item was a plain wooden chair with one short leg, and a woman named Dana came every day for a week to ask for it. Grant refused each time. He said it was promised to a collector; later he said it was not for sale; finally he simply pretended not to hear her. I thought him stubborn, even petty. On Friday I learned that the chair had stood in the room where Dana's brother had stayed as a novice, and that Grant had been searching all week for the matching short-legged table.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Grant over the course of the passage?
options: Steady admiration, since the narrator always trusts Grant's judgment about selling items.
Initial disapproval that gives way to recognition of a motive the narrator had not seen.
Growing suspicion that Grant is hiding the chair in order to sell it at a higher price.
Lasting amusement at Grant's refusals, which the narrator treats as a running joke.
items.explanation: 화자는 Grant가 Dana의 요청을 계속 거절하자 그를 고집스럽고 옹졸하다고 여긴다. 그러나 금요일에 그 의자가 Dana의 오빠가 머물던 방의 것이며 Grant가 짝이 되는 탁자를 찾고 있었다는 사실을 알게 된다. 따라서 처음의 못마땅함이 몰랐던 동기에 대한 인식으로 바뀐다는 B가 정답이다. A는 초반의 부정적 평가와, C의 의심과 D의 재미는 지문의 근거와 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: After midnight the pharmacy in Accra was nearly silent, and Adaeze worked the counter alone until Kofi arrived with the letter. He had been her father's closest friend, and he had translated the letter her father sent from Lagos years ago, the one that said he would not return. Now Kofi set the original beside her register. "I told you he chose to stay," he said. "His words were closer to 'I am not permitted to leave.' I thought that softer meaning would keep you waiting forever." Adaeze read the Yoruba lines slowly, the way she checked a prescription. For a decade she had answered his birthdays with silence. A taxi idled outside, its radio playing highlife, while a moth circled the blue sign above the door.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the passage?
options: To recount a night when Adaeze worked alone at a pharmacy until an old friend visited her.
To describe the strict procedures Adaeze follows when checking customers' prescriptions late at night.
To suggest that honesty is always the best choice, even when the truth may cause pain.
To show how learning a letter's true wording forces Adaeze to reconsider years of resentment.
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 두 곳의 근거를 합쳐 요지를 잡아야 하고, 오답 하나는 일화 요약에 그치는 부분 요지다
items.explanation: Kofi는 아버지의 편지를 '스스로 남기로 했다'고 번역했지만 실제로는 '떠나는 것이 허락되지 않는다'는 뜻이었다고 고백한다. 이어 Adaeze가 원문을 천천히 읽고 지난 10년 동안 아버지의 생일 인사에 침묵으로 답해 왔다는 사실이 드러나, 그녀가 오랜 원망을 다시 생각하게 됨을 암시한다. 따라서 D가 정답이다. A는 일화만 요약했고, B는 지문 소재를 쓰지만 목적이 다르며, C는 지나치게 일반적인 교훈이다.

items.passage: "Your heel is worn on the left, as it always was," said Anacleto, without lifting his eyes from the awl. Pavel had set the boot on the counter of the little stall in Oaxaca and waited, as if nine years were a matter that required no remark. In their youth the two men had baked on opposite corners of the same street, each rising earlier to spite the other, each claiming the better crust. Now Anacleto mended shoes, and Pavel, it seemed, had come back with nothing but a cracked boot. Neither spoke of the ovens or of the winter Pavel vanished. Yet when the work was done, Anacleto refused the coins, and Pavel, after a long moment, left on the counter a small loaf wrapped in paper, still warm. Outside, a cart of marigolds rattled past toward the market, its driver singing off-key.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To show two former rivals renewing a bond through gestures, not explanations
To recount how a baker who vanished for years came back to have a boot repaired
To explain why Anacleto abandoned baking and took up the trade of mending shoes
To suggest that old quarrels always fade once enough years have quietly passed

items.passage: When Hassan and I first climbed the wall of the abandoned orchard behind his father's rental houses in Colombo, we were twelve and wanted only mangoes. Within a summer we had cleared the weeds, propped the sagging trees, and sold enough fruit at the junction to pay my family's rent for a month. I remember that I was proud, and that Hassan was prouder. But success has a way of being noticed. His father began asking what the orchard earned, and my mother began worrying aloud that we owed him for every mango. Hassan and I still met under the trees, though now we counted the fruit before we talked. Haoran, my younger brother, stopped coming with us altogether. Years later, I still keep a bent pruning hook on a nail by my door, its handle wrapped in blue electrical tape.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe how two children cleared an overgrown orchard and sold its mangoes
To reflect on how a shared success drew a friendship into two families' tensions
To argue that the orchard's owner, not his tenants' children, should have restored it
To suggest that every childhood friendship eventually yields to adult concerns

items.passage: Auckland summers, in my memory, smelled of hot tar and of the rooftop water tank where I hid after my father left. Kainoa, who sold fish from the back of a van on our street, found me there one afternoon holding my father's old diving watch, its strap cracked. He did not ask about it. Instead he handed me a snapper to carry home and said the watch still kept good time. For weeks afterward he timed his deliveries by it, calling up to the roof for the hour, as though the watch had a job worth doing. I began to wind it each morning without being told. Kamal, my cousin, thought the whole arrangement ridiculous. Below the tank, the neighbor's lemon tree dropped its fruit into the gutter, and nobody gathered it.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

items.passage: On her first morning in Rotterdam, Hana stood in the customs line with her boots tied to her duffel bag, the same boots she had barely worn all last season on the bench. Lars, her new coach, waited beyond the glass with a club scarf folded over his arm. When the officer asked the purpose of her visit, Hana said work, then corrected herself and said football. Months earlier she had told a reporter that she no longer knew what she was for. At the gate, Lars offered to carry the duffel, but Hana shook her head and slung it over her own shoulder, boots knocking against her back. items.passage: Who leaves a recipe tin buried under a ferry terminal? Kalani asked herself this as she knelt in the sand the storm had stripped from around the pilings on Maui. The tin was rusted, but inside, wrapped in oilcloth, were cards in her grandmother's slanted hand. Aunt Mattie, who ran the terminal snack counter and allowed no one else near her stove, had always said there were no family recipes, only work. Kalani turned one card over and found Mattie's own childhood initials penciled in a corner beside a smear of what might have been coconut. She tucked the tin into her apron instead of carrying it straight to her aunt, and that afternoon she cooked the first recipe alone, before Mattie's shift began. Gulls circled the docked ferry, waiting for the passengers' scraps.
items.question: Based on the text, why does Kalani most likely cook the recipe before her aunt arrives?

items.passage: After the rains ended, Zawadi went to the seed cooperative in Nairobi to collect his late grandfather's share, and Neema, who had sorted beans beside the old man for forty years, met him at the door with a ledger. They argued first about the jar labels, which Zawadi wanted printed and Neema insisted on writing by hand. Her voice was sharp, but she kept touching the shelf where his grandfather's chair had stood. Zawadi noticed that she had saved the speckled cowpeas his grandfather favored in a separate tin, tied with the same frayed string he had always used. When he finally conceded the labels, Neema laughed softly and pressed the tin into his hands without a word. He stood holding it, feeling its weight shift as the seeds settled. In the yard, a boy was chasing a goat between the drying racks.

### lit40-medium-06-085 — skill text_structure_purpose · 유형 tone_shift

A drawer of lead type slid open with a groan when Hamza needed the letter that, in our shared wall's language of knocks, meant come over. I had lived beside his printing press in Beirut for six years and knew its moods: the thump of the platen, the hiss of the ink roller, the mutter of a man who disliked every street map he had ever printed. That evening he spread a new one across his table and jabbed at the errors, a missing alley here, a renamed square there, until I, Mehreen, began to defend the city's mapmakers out of pure stubbornness. Then he traced a faint pencil line I had not noticed. It ran from my door to his, through the plaster. "This," he said, "they always leave out." I stopped arguing.

[질문] Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the passage?
A) It shifts from bitter resentment to forgiveness as the narrator finally pardons Hamza's many insults.
B) It shifts from bickering humor to quiet tenderness when Hamza reveals the line between their homes.
C) It shifts from nostalgic longing to practical urgency as the neighbors correct the map's mistakes.
D) It shifts from fearful suspicion to trust when the narrator learns the purpose of the knocking.

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]
앞부분은 Hamza가 지도의 오류를 찌르고 화자가 고집으로 지도 제작자를 변호하는 티격태격하는 유머가 중심이다. 그러나 Hamza가 화자의 집에서 자기 집으로 이어지는 연필 선을 보여 주며 '그들은 늘 이걸 빼먹는다'고 말하자 화자는 말다툼을 멈춘다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A의 원한과 D의 의심은 지문에 없고, C는 결말의 정서를 잘못 짚었다.

Three things were forbidden in the Gdansk library where my aunt Ksenia worked: food, whispering, and the name Dmitri. I was fifteen, cooking her dinners that winter, and I broke the first rule constantly, smuggling dumplings in my coat to eat between the stacks. Ksenia scolded me in her flat librarian's voice and confiscated them with the same efficiency she used for overdue books. I thought her made of index cards. One evening, shelving a returned atlas, I found a slip tucked inside: a borrower's card, decades old, signed Dmitri in a child's looping script. Beneath it, in Ksenia's neat hand, someone had renewed the loan every year. I carried it to her desk. She looked at it for a long time, and her voice, when it came, was barely a whisper.

[질문] Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the passage?

[표시된 정답] C
[해설]
앞부분에서 화자는 만두를 몰래 들여오고 고모를 '색인 카드로 만든 사람'이라 여기는 등 고모의 엄격함을 가볍게 비꼰다. 그러나 매년 대출이 연장된 Dmitri의 오래된 카드를 발견하고, 엄격하던 고모가 겨우 속삭이듯 말하는 장면에서 숨겨진 슬픔을 엄숙하게 깨닫는 어조로 바뀐다. 따라서 C가 정답이다. A는 반항, B는 의심으로 잘못 해석했고, D는 순서와 정서가 모두 반대다.
### lit40-medium-06-087 — skill text_structure_purpose · 유형 text_structure

Spools of thread rattled in Baoyu's tin as she climbed into the old projection booth above the shuttered cinema in Chengdu, where she had sewn costumes for twenty years. Hari, her only apprentice, was already there, pinning hems by the dusty window. The theater's owner had sold the building; one of them could follow him to his new shop across the river, and one could not. Baoyu had rehearsed the speech for days. Instead, she watched Hari work. He knotted thread the way she had taught him, then in a way she hadn't, a small twist that held better than hers. She remembered her own teacher, decades earlier, watching her the same way before stepping aside. When the owner climbed the stairs, Baoyu set the tin of spools in Hari's hands and turned to the projector.

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?
A) It describes a conflict between two workers, then shows them agreeing to share a new shop.
B) It presents the long history of a cinema, then explains why its owner decided to sell the building.
C) It contrasts two sewing techniques, then argues that the older method is superior.
D) It introduces a difficult choice, then traces the observations that lead Baoyu to resolve it.

[표시된 정답] D
[해설]
지문은 둘 중 한 명만 주인을 따라갈 수 있다는 어려운 선택을 먼저 제시한다. 이어 Baoyu가 Hari의 바느질을 지켜보며 그의 실력을 확인하고, 자신의 스승이 물러나던 기억을 떠올린 뒤 실패 통을 Hari에게 건넨다. 따라서 선택과 그 해결로 이끄는 관찰을 따라간다는 D가 정답이다. A의 공유, B의 극장 역사, C의 기법 우열 주장은 지문 구조와 맞지 않는다.

By noon the line at Matteo's noodle stall in Bologna stretched past the fountain, and every customer obeyed the sign nailed above the counter: one bowl per person, no exceptions. Caio, who had taught Matteo arithmetic forty years before, reached the front and asked for two. Matteo pointed at the sign without looking up. "Rules are rules, maestro." Caio nodded, paid for one, and stepped aside. He did not leave. Instead he stood by the fountain and gave his bowl, untouched, to a boy whose mother had been turned away for asking the same thing. Matteo watched the boy eat. Then he watched the next customer, a widow with two grandchildren, reach the counter. He reached up, pried the sign loose, and slid it under the cash drawer, where flour soon covered it.

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?
A) It establishes a rigid rule, shows a quiet act that exposes its cost, and ends with the rule being abandoned.
B) It describes a busy market, then shifts to a lengthy debate between two former classmates about the fairness of the stall's prices.
C) It recounts a teacher's lesson from the past, then shows a student applying it decades later.
D) It introduces a popular stall, then explains the economic reasons for limiting customers' orders.

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
지문은 '한 사람당 한 그릇'이라는 엄격한 규칙으로 시작한다. 이어 Caio가 자신의 그릇을 거절당한 소년에게 건네는 조용한 행동으로 규칙의 대가를 드러내고, 마지막에 Matteo가 간판을 떼어 내 규칙을 포기한다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B의 가격 논쟁, C의 과거 수업 회상, D의 경제적 이유 설명은 지문에 나오지 않는다.

She filled the cracks with a gold-tinted resin and set the bowl on the kiln shelf to cure. For weeks I ignored it. Then Ximena, the studio's owner, asked me to carry it to the display window. In the afternoon light the seams looked less like damage than like a map. I still believe some things cannot be repaired. I have also kept the bowl on my desk for nine years.

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?

When the Surabaya market opened at dawn, Arisa unrolled her mother's batik across the stall table before the fruit sellers had even lifted their shutters. Her mother, too weak now to walk the aisles, still drew the patterns each night in wax by lamplight, and Arisa dyed and sold them. Customers stopped all morning. They traced the waxy borders with their fingertips, called the work extraordinary, and photographed it for their cousins abroad. __A tourist asked whether the artist would sign one, then left without buying anything.__ By noon Arisa had sold two small scarves, enough for rice and her mother's medicine but not for the new wax. ### lit40-medium-07-006 — skill inferences · 유형 tone_or_mood
[지문]
After the rains ended, Zawadi went to the seed cooperative in Nairobi to collect his late grandfather's share, and Neema, who had sorted beans beside the old man for forty years, met him at the door with a ledger. They argued first about the jar labels, which Zawadi wanted printed and Neema insisted on writing by hand. Her voice was sharp, but she kept touching the shelf where his grandfather's chair had stood. Zawadi noticed that she had saved the speckled cowpeas his grandfather favored in a separate tin, tied with the same frayed string he had always used. When he finally conceded the labels, Neema laughed softly and pressed the tin into his hands without a word. He stood holding it, feeling its weight shift as the seeds settled. In the yard, a boy was chasing a goat between the drying racks.

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
A) Irritable, dwelling on a stubborn quarrel over how the jar labels should be written
B) Tender, with brief surface bickering giving way to shared grief and affection
C) Combative, though softened at moments by small hints of fondness between the two
D) Celebratory, reflecting the cooperative's pride in a plentiful harvest after the rains

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]
라벨을 두고 다투는 장면과 날카로운 목소리에는 짜증이 드러나지만, Neema가 할아버지 의자가 있던 선반을 계속 만지고 그가 좋아하던 콩을 따로 챙겨 둔 장면에서는 슬픔과 애정이 더 두드러진다. 따라서 표면의 다툼이 공유된 슬픔과 애정으로 이어지는 다정한 어조라는 B가 정답이다. A는 덜 두드러진 정서만 말했고, C는 두 정서의 비중을 뒤집었다. D는 비가 그쳤다는 소재와 어울리지만 지문에 단서가 약하다.
